query: Consider the following context: The recent trend of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) was studied extensively for their promising mechanical properties, but individual constituents' effects have remained unexplored. In that context, which method can be used for the effects of changing the percentage of elements of HfNbTaTiZr-HEA on the mechanical properties, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Using high‐throughput combinatorial processing to create a continuous composition gradient in HfNbTaTiZr can reveal individual constituent effects, and specifically, increasing the Hf content will enhance mechanical strength (e.g., higher hardness and yield strength) compared to the equimolar baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: An equimolar HfNbTaTiZr high‐entropy alloy with a well‐characterized microstructure and mechanical properties (e.g., hardness, yield strength) from conventional processing.
generation.intervention: Employing additive manufacturing or combinatorial sputtering to produce samples with a controlled gradient in elemental composition, specifically varying the Hf percentage while adjusting the relative amounts of the other elements to maintain overall alloy integrity.
generation.conditions: Ambient to moderately elevated temperature conditions during rapid mechanical screening (using techniques such as nanoindentation or mini-tensile testing) while ensuring phase stability through precise process control.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized microstructural modifications, such as grain refinement or changes in lattice distortion and dislocation pinning, that arise from variations in the Hf content.
generation.mechanism: An increased percentage of Hf is predicted to enhance lattice distortions and mismatch, which act as barriers to dislocation motion, thereby improving hardness and strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: A systematic correlation is expected: locales with higher Hf content will exhibit measurable increases in hardness and possibly yield strength (with an anticipated relative change in the order of 10-20% compared to the equimolar baseline), provided the phase remains a stable solid solution.
generation.baseline: The equimolar HfNbTaTiZr alloy processed via conventional methods with known microstructural and mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: This relationship holds as long as the compositional variations remain within the phase stability and solubility limits of the alloy system; excessive deviation may lead to formation of brittle intermetallic phases or phase separation.
generation.uncertainty: While the direction of the change (an increase in strength with higher Hf content) is expected based on atomic size and lattice distortion effects, the exact magnitude of the mechanical property enhancement is uncertain and will depend on microstructural evolution, processing parameters, and possible secondary phase formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of HfNbTaTiZr samples with a continuous gradient in composition using additive manufacturing (or combinatorial sputtering). Map the local mechanical properties (via nanoindentation and/or mini-tensile tests) along the gradient. Compare the measured properties with the baseline equimolar alloy processed under identical conditions.
measurements: Phase analysis (XRD or electron microscopy) to confirm phase stability across the gradient
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the measured mechanical properties (e.g., hardness and yield strength) do not exhibit a systematic increase with increasing Hf content or if the microstructural analysis shows that the observed property changes result from phase instabilities (e.g., formation of brittle intermetallic compounds) rather than the intended lattice distortion effects, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High entropy alloys (HEA) have been one of the most attractive groups of materials for researchers in the last several years. Since HEAs are potential candidates for many (e.g., refractory, cryogenic, medical) applications, their properties are studied intensively. The most frequent method of HEA synthesis is arc or induction melting. Powder metallurgy is a perspective technique of alloy synthesis and therefore in this work the possibilities of synthesis of HfNbTaTiZr HEA from powders were studied. Blended elemental powders were sintered, hot isostatically pressed, and subsequently swaged using a special technique of swaging where the sample is enveloped by a titanium alloy. This method does not result in a full density alloy due to cracking during swaging. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed powders resulted in a fully dense but brittle specimen. The most promising result was obtained by SPS treatment of gas atomized powder with low oxygen content. The microstructure of HfNbTaTiZr specimen prepared this way can be refined by high pressure torsion deformation resulting in a high hardness of 410 HV10 and very fine microstructure with grain size well below 5

Abstract High entropy or compositionally complex alloys provide opportunities for optimization towards new high-temperature materials. Improvements in the equiatomic alloy Al 17 Co 17 Cr 17 Cu 17 Fe 17 Ni 17 (at.%) led to the base alloy for this work with the chemical composition Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (at.%). Characterization of the beneficial particle-strengthened microstructure by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and observation of good mechanical properties at elevated temperatures arose the need of accomplishing further optimization steps. For this purpose, the refractory metals hafnium and molybdenum were added in small amounts (0.5 and 1.0 at.% respectively) because of their well-known positive effects on mechanical properties of Ni-based superalloys. By correlation of microstructural examinations using SEM with tensile tests in the temperature range of room temperature up to 900 °C, conclusions could be drawn for further optimization steps. Keywords: HEA, high entropy alloys, compositionally complex alloys, mechanical characterization
